newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Iraq calls on Middle East states to reveal arms.
newsitem.headline: Iraq calls on Middle East states to reveal arms.

text.p: Iraq, saying it had cooperated with the United Nations in disarming itself under terms of the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire, on Thursday called for all Middle East states to openly declare their weapons of mass destruction.

Barzan Ibrahim Al-Tikriti -- half-brother of Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein who serves as his country's ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva -- made the appeal in a speech to the Conference on Disarmament.
He also urged the 61-member forum to launch stalled negotiations for global treaties to ban anti-personnel landmines and production of nuclear bomb-making fissile material.
The Middle East region contained roughly half of the landmines in the world, according to the Iraqi envoy.

Iraq was "transparent" about implementing Security Council resolutions on weapons of mass destruction, presenting regular periodic data and statements on the activities relating to such weapons, according to Barzan.

"That is why Iraq, because of concern about national security, and on the basis of what has happened, requests that all the neighbouring countries and other parties in the Middle East follow the principles of transparency by openly declaring all their weapons including mass destruction weapons and their means of delivery," he said.
There was no reaction from Israel, which like Iraq was admitted to the main multilateral disarmament negotiating body in June 1996, nor from any other state of the volatile region.
Iraq's record of compliance on disarmament issues has been mixed at best in the wake of its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Last June, Iraq barred U.N. inspectors from entering three sensitive sites, prompting the Security Council to issue a unanimous resolution warning Baghdad that it would face further sanctions if it blocked U.N. inspectors. Iraq rejected the resolution, saying it was unjustified.
A team of eight U.N. ballistic missile experts arrived in Baghdad on Monday for a two-week mission to investigate whether Iraq still had any banned weapons.

The U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) was charged with disarming Iraq under terms of the Gulf War ceasefire conditions and continues to check for weapons of mass destruction and ensure they are not replaced.

UNSCOM must certify that Iraq has no weapons of mass destruction before the United Nations will lift curbs on the country's oil exports, although Baghdad is allowed limited sales under a humanitarian deal.
